rows.Problem Statement: Senate interns and intern coordinators are unsupported
rows.Problem Description: The House Intern Resource Office (HIRO), created from a Select Committee on Modernization recommendation, is the House's central hub for internships, handling onboarding, professional development, coordinator training, and institution-wide data collection. The Senate has no equivalent, so each office builds its program in isolation. Internship quality depends entirely on where an intern lands, and the institution cannot say how many unpaid interns it hosts or offer demographic data beyond what payroll disclosures incidentally capture.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Senate Intern Resource Office
rows.Solution Description: Fund a Senate Intern Resource Office as the chamber's counterpart to HIRO, giving interns and the staffers who manage them consistent onboarding and professional development, and maintaining records on intern numbers, pay, and demographics—work that has fallen to outside organizations by default. Use would be voluntary, preserving each Senator's authority over their own program while ensuring no office has to start from scratch. It should be Senate-specific rather than an extension of HIRO, since the chambers run on different rules and traditions.
rows.Horizon Justification: Interns are the Senate's main talent pipeline, and this strengthen the pipeline from the start.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Karen Gibson asked the Leg Branch Approps subcommittee for funding to launch this initiative with two FTEs in FY2025. However, no funding has been dedicated to it.

headers: Support agencies are scaled for a slower, less technical era
CRS, CBO, and GAO are real institutions doing real work, but their resourcing, structure, and product formats were designed for the volume, speed, and technical complexity of a previous decade.
Support agencies operate at the speed and technical depth of the questions Congress now faces

The legislative branch's analytical institutions are resourced and organized for current demand, carry deep technical expertise in house, and deliver answers on the timeline a member actually needs them.
Risk-conservative culture, “independence theater,” and the absence of any protected space for legislative-branch R&D mean innovations die inside support agencies and never reach Congress.
Create a DARPA-like independent innovation unit for the legislative branch

Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style independence (insulated from host-agency risk aversion) with a mandate to ship demos to members and staff, showcase NLP/AI work, and de-risk ideas through crawl-walk-run pilots.

Structural independence from host-agency risk culture changes the condition producing the problem rather than routing around it. A standing unit with its own mandate to ship to members creates permanent institutional capability that survives any individual champion.
Concept only; STAA exists but constrained by GAO risk culture

rows.CRS, CBO, GAO, LOC: Personal Office, Professional Development, Operations, CAO
rows.Support agencies are scaled for a slower: Constituent service runs on tools and support built for a slower tempo
rows.CRS, CBO, and GAO are real institutions: Casework and constituent mail are handled with systems and training that have not kept pace with the volume, speed, and complexity constituents now expect, and much of the support that does exist is supplied from outside the institution.
rows.Support agencies operate at the speed an: Constituent service is a fast, well-supported institutional function
rows.The legislative branch's analytical inst: Caseworkers have modern tools, permanent training, and a standing institutional network. Cases resolve at the pace constituents expect, and the patterns that surface in casework feed back into oversight and legislating.
rows.Pervasive risk aversion blocks experimen: Bill drafting and the US Code pipeline are archaic and opaque
rows.Risk-conservative culture, “independence: Staff cannot easily see how bill text modifies the US Code; the Leg Counsel / floor / GPO handoff is messy and manual (e.g., Senate clerk annotates changes in pencil; 8-hour overnight conference read-throughs of THUD).
rows.Create a DARPA-like independent innovati: Build an “Overleaf for legislation” demo tool
rows.Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style: A lightweight tool that shows how a bill written in English “compiles” into changes to the US Code, giving drafters and reviewers a live diff view; positioned as a demo to build appetite for deeper reform.
rows.Structural independence from host-agency: A demo makes the pipeline legible to the people who see it, but the statutory chain of custody, manual handoffs, and absence of version control continue unchanged underneath. It is positioned explicitly as appetite-building rather than as infrastructure.
rows.Y: Treat the demo as the first commit: have Leg Counsel or a support office adopt the diff view as a supported drafting tool with a named owner and a maintenance line, so it becomes the on-ramp to version-controlled statute instead of a proof of concept that stays one.
rows.Concept only; STAA exists but constraine: Not built; identified as a low-lift proof of concept

rows.Support agencies are scaled for a slower: Public input into Congress is low quality
rows.CRS, CBO, and GAO are real institutions: Participation mostly diffuses tension rather than informing lawmaking. Offices lack the capacity to process input at scale, and deep distrust of representation means what does arrive rarely carries usable signal.
rows.Support agencies operate at the speed an: Public input is structured signal that shapes legislation
rows.The legislative branch's analytical inst: Deliberation at scale produces clear, weighted signal about what constituents want and which tradeoffs they will accept. Commitments made in public are tracked over time, and a member can see how input moved a bill.
rows.Pervasive risk aversion blocks experimen: Tech approval and procurement pipelines are clogged and fragmented
rows.Risk-conservative culture, “independence: Offices wait months for tool approvals (Civic ~8 months; 30 days just for responses); there is no channel to aggregate demand across offices; internal dev requires “finished” projects up front; House and Senate run separate, inconsistent vendor processes.
rows.Create a DARPA-like independent innovati: Reform vendor approval and create a demand-aggregation pipeline
rows.Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style: Fast-track review lanes for low-risk tools, a portal where offices can request/upvote workflows (“50 offices asked for this”), pre-negotiated security reviews shared across chambers, and agile (not waterfall) requirements for internal builds.
rows.Structural independence from host-agency: Faster lanes and a demand portal shorten wait times inside the existing procurement structure, but the bicameral duplication and the absence of any institution-wide owner survive intact. Offices get tools sooner; Congress does not get a different way of acquiring them.
rows.Y: Give the portal teeth: make aggregated office demand automatically trigger a funded procurement, and make a single security review binding on both chambers, so approvals accumulate into shared infrastructure instead of resetting office by office.
rows.Concept only; STAA exists but constraine: Recognized problem; no unified process exists

rows.Support agencies operate at the speed an: A permanent technical corps sits inside Congress
rows.The legislative branch's analytical inst: Standing in-house technical expertise across offices and committees, with career paths, pay scales, and hiring authorities that make technical work a normal congressional career rather than a borrowed exception.

rows.Risk-conservative culture, “independence: Duplicated bicameral infrastructure, turf wars, and the absence of an institution-wide owner of modernization stifle technology adoption at scale.
rows.Create a DARPA-like independent innovati: Establish a unified congressional digital service with integrated bicameral infrastructure
rows.Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style: Evolve HDS plus a new Senate digital service into a single congressional digital service; integrate IT infrastructure across House, Senate, AOC, LOC, GPO, and committees; governed by a joint committee on technology.
rows.Structural independence from host-agency: Merging House and Senate delivery capacity into one governed institution changes the underlying structure rather than accelerating the current one. It creates a permanent owner for modernization, and the absence of that owner is what regenerates the problem.

rows.Support agencies are scaled for a slower: Congress cannot tell whether the laws it passes are working
rows.CRS, CBO, and GAO are real institutions: No standing function tracks implementation, maps how a regulatory regime actually operates, or feeds what is learned back into legislating, so oversight lags the systems it governs by years.
rows.The legislative branch's analytical inst: Learning whether a law works is a standing function of the branch. Implementation is tracked as a matter of course, findings return to the committees that wrote the law, and Congress can adapt statute continuously without institutional crisis.
rows.Pervasive risk aversion blocks experimen: Congress cannot keep pace with the executive branch's information and AI advantage
rows.Risk-conservative culture, “independence: The executive branch has more money, technical expertise, and faster procurement; oversight is adversarial and slow; Congress is bypassed in emergencies because notification takes too long; executive AI use is opaque.
rows.Create a DARPA-like independent innovati: Deploy AI-powered oversight dashboards and an AI-log subpoena regime
rows.Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style: Privacy-preserving AI systems continuously monitor executive activity (including classified domains) and alert relevant committees via dashboards; mandate AI chat logs as federal records subject to congressional subpoena, with workflows designed to avoid driving use underground.
rows.Structural independence from host-agency: Continuous monitoring plus a records regime shifts oversight from episodic and adversarial to structural, attacking the information asymmetry itself rather than compensating for it after the fact. Early stage, but it builds standing capability rather than one-time findings.
rows.Concept only; STAA exists but constraine: Early research/proposal stage (Forethought-Oxford implementation work; IAPS drafting bill text)

rows.The legislative branch's analytical inst: Policy is stress-tested against thousands of edge cases before enactment. Due diligence moves from anecdote to evidence as a working standard inside drafting and markup, not a mandate to be checked off.

rows.Create a DARPA-like independent innovati: Build a congressional intelligence platform over support-agency content
rows.Give an STAA-like body true DARPA-style: Convert GAO/CRS/CBO content into RAG-ready formats (markdown wiki) and expose a secure AI assistant that members and staff can query from their phones, including sensitive material under existing GAO protocols; release internal tools (e.g., GAO's style/partisan-tilt checker) as open source.
rows.Structural independence from host-agency: Converting support-agency output into queryable infrastructure changes how institutional knowledge reaches staff, not merely how much of it exists. The expertise is already funded; this turns it into a permanent, usable asset the institution owns.
rows.Concept only; STAA exists but constraine: Prototype-feasible; GAO has internal RAG experiments that never reached the Hill
